title: Why Isn't My Shower Diverter Working?

seo.title: Why Isn't My Shower Diverter Working?
seo.meta_description: A diverter that will not send full flow to the shower may have mineral buildup, worn seals, or a broken internal mechanism.

excerpt: A diverter that will not send full flow to the shower may have mineral buildup, worn seals, or a broken internal mechanism. content_html:
A diverter that will not send full flow to the shower may have mineral buildup, worn seals, or a broken internal mechanism. A common sign is water continuing from the tub spout after the shower is selected. Before replacing parts, identify whether the diverter is in the spout, a three-way valve, or integrated into the control.

Identify the diverter type

A pull-up tub-spout diverter is serviced differently from a lever in the valve. Photograph the assembly and look for a brand or model. Do not dismantle the main control before locating a reliable water shutoff.

Partial diversion can come from scale or a worn seal

Move the diverter with water off and see whether it is stiff or fails to reach its position. On parts that are user-removable according to the manual, cleaning scale may help; a torn seal or loose mechanism needs replacement.

A tub spout diverter is often replaced as an assembly

If the gate inside a tub spout is badly worn, replacing the whole spout may be more reliable than rebuilding it. Confirm whether it is threaded or held by a set screw and do not twist piping inside the wall with excessive force.

An internal valve requires shutting water off before opening it

Cartridges or diverters behind trim are connected to pressurized plumbing. Shut water off, verify flow has stopped, and follow the manufacturer's parts diagram. If the valve cannot be isolated or there is corrosion inside the wall, use a plumber.
